name: Wendy Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the order-disputes row at a small medical-supply contact centre called Ardent Supply. If a clinic says oxygen tubing or a box of dressings never arrived, I check the dispatch scan and phone the depot before we issue a replacement. I have a two-year college diploma and am very good at tracing lost orders, but our small company's team-lead pay is low.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI during that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day I ask the draft tool to sort the delivery notes, then I check every time and address myself. It saves me searching through ten screens. My partner Dev drives a bus on changing hours; we have only two weeks of expenses saved and our grown son lives independently.

say: I would welcome **faster note searches** while checking dispatch scans myself.
I would keep **depot contact** for a missing medical order.
think: I expect my **lead row** to remain paid in this mild picture.
I fear **two weeks saved** and variable bus hours leave rent exposed.
do: Keep **paid order disputes** and verify AI summaries against scans.
Cancel the **unused sports package** and place its fee in the rent envelope.
feel: **Anxious** about current rent, though the AI change itself is small.
S0.quote: A box of dressings does not reach a clinic because the screen says delivered.
fieldNote: She uses AI **daily** but verifies each draft against dispatch records.
Her high skill cannot erase **two-week savings** and variable household wages.
The small package cut helps the **next rent payment** without claiming financial safety.

steps.text: Keep paid order-dispute calls and verify AI summaries against depot scans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues a faster note search helps if we still verify the dispatch scan. A box of dressings does not reach a clinic because the screen says delivered. I would keep the depot number by the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead row and ordinary pay survive this mild picture. Our two-week reserve is the problem already, and Dev's bus hours are uneven. Even if AI adds little, one short pay week could put our rent behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep handling paid disputes and checking every AI summary against the scan as I do today. This year Dev and I would cancel the unused sports package and put that fee into the rent envelope. In the first year of this picture I'd work the same paid rota and review our actual weekly income each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about household cash, though not frightened by this AI picture. Two weeks saved is too close to the rent due date. I feel better when we know exactly what each shift paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cancel the sports package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The package has stayed on the bill because neither of us got around to cancelling it. We can watch the free matches with our son when he visits. I would not pretend the fee makes us secure, but it adds a little room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown son has his own rent. We would tell him we're watching our budget, not ask him to pay it. I need verified later-life income before I could talk about dropping paid shifts.

say: I would demand **traceable delivery decisions** before a case closes.
I would ask for **paid correction time** when the new screen gets a scan wrong.
think: I can learn the **new exception screen** but may still lose paid hours.
I cannot fund a **long search** from two weeks saved.
do: Attend the **approved paid session** on the new AI exception screen and practise three cases.
Keep **paid disputes** and record where the screen fails.
Stop **monthly takeaway** only if paid hours fall; compare posted local jobs by full-week wages and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss despite curiosity about the tool.
S1.quote: I can learn quickly, but I cannot learn a missing pay packet into existence.
fieldNote: She commits to **new screen learning**, beyond ordinary daily AI checks.
She expects **paid hours** might shrink even if she masters the tool.
The takeaway cut waits for **actual rota loss**, not a forecast.

steps.text: Attend approved paid AI exception-screen session and practise three wrong-delivery cases
Keep paid dispute calls and record new-screen errors
Stop monthly takeaway only after actual paid-hour cuts
Compare few posted local service jobs by full-week wages and hours after hour cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the new system should show its work when it claims a delivery arrived. I'd demonstrate the bad scans to the other agents and ask the employer to pay for time to correct them. A clinic should not have to call twice because an answer arrived too quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take the easy order calls and management might cut our paid row. I can learn the new exception screen faster than most here, but that is not a promise of hours. Our rent cannot wait while a small company decides what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd take the approved one-hour session on the new AI exception screen and practise opening three wrong-delivery cases on paid time. I'd keep the paid dispute queue and note where the new screen fails. If my hours actually fall over the next few years, Dev and I would stop the monthly takeaway and I would compare the few posted local service jobs by full-week wages and hours; in the first year I'd keep available calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the row and wages, even while I'm curious about the tool. I can learn quickly, but I cannot learn a missing pay packet into existence. We have almost no cash room for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is new about the exception screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new AI screen connects the scan, warehouse note and customer's complaint in one place. I'd learn its exception button and test it on three cases, not just keep doing the old lookup. Then I'd show colleagues what it got right and wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you stop the takeaway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the rota proves we have lost paid hours. Takeaway is pleasant but rent comes first. I would not borrow against an imagined new service job.

I would say **2031 robots** do not delay headset cuts.

Check the **posted paid counter** by weekly wages, hours, bus fare and safe lifting.
Apply if the row ends in 2028-29; accept only **rent-and-bill-covering wages** and hours after travel.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and an imminent rent gap.
S2.quote: I still have a list of calls to make, but a list is not a wage.
fieldNote: Her daily AI skill does not protect the **disputes wage** in fast AGI.
The local **job list** is short despite her skill and diploma.
She checks **safe lifting** and full-week pay before accepting a counter shift.

steps.text: Join three agents jointly requesting written closure dates and remaining paid hours
Check posted clinic-supply counter by weekly wages, hours, bus fare and safe lifting
Apply if row ends in 2028-29; accept only rent-and-bill-covering full-week wages/hours after travel
Keep any Ardent Supply paid dispute hours while counter application is pending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the row that full thinking AI by 2028 can sort notes and speak to clinics without us. Robots arrive later, around 2031; that does not delay a contact-centre cut. I would ask for written paid-hour and closure plans before somebody removes the queue from the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our dispute row to close in the first year after 2028, despite my skill with tools. Dev's variable bus wage cannot carry all our rent and bills, and two weeks saved will disappear fast. There are very few comparable jobs nearby, so I would be awake worrying about the first unpaid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd join three other agents in a joint request for written closure dates and any remaining paid hours. I'd check the actual posted local clinic-supply counter opening, including weekly wages, hours, bus fare and handling duties. If our dispute row ends in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for that paid position; I'd accept only if the full paid week after travel covers rent and bills, while keeping any Ardent Supply hours still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I expect the wage to go and can picture the rent date arriving before a new pay day. I still have a list of calls to make, but a list is not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the clinic-supply counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supply counter has boxes, labels and people collecting orders. I would ask whether I can do the lifting safely before taking the shift, and I won't assume robots in 2031 leave that work alone. A posted paid rota matters more than my idea of a safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Dev's bus wage carry the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would keep paid bus runs while the company has them, but the rota changes each week. We would budget from the hours actually offered, not his best month. Our son's income is his to manage.

I would test **posted stock work** before treating it as another wage.
think: I could teach **repeat-error checks** while calls still pay.
I know **2031 thinking AI** can also take training notes and screen work.
do: Request **two paid teaching sessions** using three anonymised dispute cases.
Keep **paid lead calls** and inspect posted stock shifts quarterly for safe lifting and actual weekly wages and hours.
Apply after 2031 row closure only to **posted stock-check work** with weekly wages and hours covering rent and bills after bus fare.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test a skill but no assured post.
S3.quote: Without a posted paid depot shift, I will not leave my current contact-centre wage.
fieldNote: She proposes **paid teaching** from her existing expertise, without inventing a course.
Stock-check work requires **safe lifting** and an actual paid rota.
No opening means **available calls** and reachable search, not an unpaid trial.

steps.text: Request two paid teaching sessions using three anonymised dispute cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us work out which claims a person really must verify and whether anyone will be paid to do it. I could learn the depot's physical stock checks as well as the screen side, but robots around 2034 may change those too. I would rather test a real paid shift than collect a certificate for a vanished role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use my order knowledge to become a paid trainer on error cases while the calls still come in. I still expect full AGI in 2031 to handle a lot of screen work, including training notes. Our two-week reserve means I cannot step away from a wage for an unpaid experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask Ardent Supply for two paid sessions to teach new agents the three mistakes that cause repeat delivery disputes. I'd keep my paid lead rota and check each quarter whether a real paid stock-check shift is posted. In the first year after 2031, if the dispute row closes, I'd apply for a posted stock-check role only if the weekly wage and hours after bus fare cover rent and bills; if none exists, I'd keep available paid calls and search reachable work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more organised than in the fast version. I have a skill I can show on real cases. It does not guarantee a post once a machine can do the notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach in two sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use three real dispute records with customer details removed. The supervisor would need to pay the two sessions; I am not giving away hours when the rent is due. I could show the new exception screen, but the lesson is how to check the depot before promising a clinic anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to the depot without a posted shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the stock duties for safe lifting and the actual weekly paid rota. Without a posted paid depot shift, I will not leave my current contact-centre wage. Dev and I would keep our own paid hours and not turn an unpaid trial into household income.

fieldNote: Her ability to learn AI does not solve **current rent**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers a decade is enough time to demand real staffing plans every year, not a poster about reinvention. Thinking AI reaches our order desk by 2036; robots may reach physical stock work around 2039. I would want the company to show what work it still pays people to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight I may still need paid hours; we have not verified income that would replace either wage. Two weeks saved makes this month's rent urgent even with ten years before AGI. I can learn new tools quickly, but I cannot make a cushion by calling a certificate an asset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year Dev and I would put our actual weekly pay and rent on a sheet and move the old sports-package fee into a separate rent reserve. I'd keep the paid dispute row and check any written later-income figures rather than assuming a pension. Each spring I'd join coworkers asking the company for staffing dates; if the row closes in the first year after 2036, I'd apply for a posted paid role only when full-week wages and hours after travel cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious even with a decade. I know how to learn a new screen, but the rent is due next month. A long date on the calendar does not add money to the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you actually save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when a month's actual pay leaves enough after rent and food. If Dev has fewer bus runs, we would keep the rent current and delay the savings target. I would like six months saved, but I cannot promise it on today's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son help with the later-income gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son is welcome at Sunday lunch, and we would tell him what we are doing. We won't plan on his earnings to make our own rent. If verified later income is too small, we will keep paid work in the plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even being the best at this desk cannot stretch two weeks of rent money into a long search. Written closure dates and a real paid stock or counter shift within bus reach would help. I'd need actual weekly wages and hours before I could move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the customers can challenge a delivery decision when the screen is wrong. My diploma taught me to check a record, not worship it. Someone must be paid to hear that challenge.

headlineQuote: My diploma taught me to check a record, not worship it.
portrait: Wendy is a **58-year-old** order-disputes lead with a two-year college diploma.
She uses AI **daily** and learns new screens early.
Her **lower wage**, two-week reserve and few local jobs keep rent exposed.
She asks coworkers for **written staffing plans** and tests real paid alternatives.
She expects **fast AGI** to threaten the dispute wage despite her strong skill.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when the dispute row could close before another wage appears.
whatWouldHelp: Written **closure dates** and reachable posted paid work with full weekly hours.
